H. Annexes ....................................................................................................................................... 25 A. Introduction 
Background 
The Secretary General’s Policy Committee decision on integration (2008/24 on 25 June 2008) reaffirms 
integration as the guiding principle for all conflict and post conflict situations where the UN has a Country 
Team and a multi-dimensional peace-keeping or political mission/office. The main purpose of integration is 
to maximize the individual and collective impact of the UN activities to consolidate peace in a country. The 
decision also notes that all country presences specified, of which Somalia is one, should develop an integrated 
strategic framework (ISF) in order to implement the decision’s requirements for: a shared vision of the UN’s 
Strategic Objectives; closely aligned or integrated planning; agreed results, timelines and responsibilities for 
the delivery of tasks critical to peace consolidation; and agreed mechanisms for monitoring and evaluation. 
The UN senior management in Somalia; the UN Political Office for Somalia (UNPOS), the UN Country 
Team (UNCT) and UN Support Office for AMISOM (UNSOA) held a retreat on 21-22 February 2011 to 
advance the development of the ISF for the UN system in Somalia. The ISF Somalia defines the UN’s 
priority Strategic Objectives that focus on peacebuilding across the whole of Somalia. It identifies results, 
timelines and agency responsibilities to achieve the objectives, and outlines a monitoring and evaluation 
mechanism for the framework. The ISF draws on a review of the existing UN strategies and UN Security 
Council mandates for UNPOS and UNSOA in addition to the development and humanitarian objectives of 
the UN as articulated in the UN Somali Assistance Strategy (UNSAS), and the Consolidated Appeal Process 
(CAP). The ISF is an internal UN document that allows the UN to consolidate its existing activities towards 
prioritised peacebuilding objectives, leveraging the different strengths of the UN agencies, funds, 
programmes and mission capacities to achieve them. The ISF is not a fundraising document, and is supported 
by a Joint Planning Unit (JPU) comprising representatives from UNPOS, UNSOA and the UNCT. 
The ISF will have a timeframe of one year (April 2011– March 2012). The short timeframe was determined 
by the heightened political uncertainty that exists in anticipation of the ending of the transitional period in 
August 2011. The timeframe also allows the UN to re-assess its approach to peacebuilding after the current 
transition ends, and once a new government is in place. The ISF could potentially fold into the UNSAS. 
The ISF objectives and results were developed with the view to address urgent priority needs that contribute 
to peacebuilding, and to engage the appropriate UN actors in their delivery. The results were designed to 
utilize existing resources, and to build on current or planned UN activities, hence minimizing the need for the 
creation of new projects. Protection of Civilians (PoC) and Piracy are the two main cross cutting themes 
reflected across most of the results and tasks. 
2B. Conflict Analysis 
Somalia’s twenty years of conflict have led to the destruction of much of the country’s infrastructure. The 
conflict has created over 1.5 million Somali refugees, and the displacement of 1.4 additional Somalis within 
the country. Currently, as a result of drought as well as conflict, an estimated one third of the population are 
in need of emergency assistance, while one in four children in southern Somalia are acutely malnourished. 
Rangeland degradation and restrictions on movement resulting from conflict are creating vulnerability and 
destitution in Somalia’s pastoralist population who constitute an estimated 60 percent of the total population. 
The main areas of armed conflict are concentrated in and around southern Somalia where the fertile riverine 
valleys remain the most valuable land in the country. Mogadishu remains the epicenter of conflict and 
Somalia’s southern port city of Kismayo the secondary focus of conflict. Although Somalia’s conflict has 
domestic origins, external actors have frequently been central protagonists either as international peace 
enforcement or protection forces or occupying armies engaged in proxy wars. External engagement in 
Somalia’s conflict has also involved covert counter terrorist operations. Externally driven aid and trade 
activities have also contributed to Somalia’s conflicts. 
Since the downfall of Siad Barre twenty years ago, Somalia has experienced various weak or absent central 
governments. While the absence of public order and rule of law has been a central factor in the country’s 
vulnerability to conflict over the past two decades, it has also been argued that the establishment of an 
imposed central state model is at the heart of the Somali problem. Nonetheless, parts of the country have 
enjoyed relative peace and security for extended periods of time without a central state. In some instances 
efforts to revive the central state have triggered armed clashes. 
Following the Mbagathi/Eldoret process which established the Transitional Federal Institutions in 2004, the 
UN initiated the current Djibouti peace process in 2007 as a means to broaden the political base of the 
Transitional Federal Government to include former elements of the Union of Islamic Courts. Following 
Presidential elections in 2008, a new Transitional Federal Government was established in January 2009 with a 
mandate through 20 August 2011. The TFG’s attempts to further broaden the political and reconciliation 
base has yielded limited results so far. 
In 2008 the UN Security Council supported the deployment of the African Union peacekeeping force 
(AMISOM) to Mogadishu to support the TFG and consolidate security and stability in Somalia. AMISOM 
managed to support the TFG in securing some of the most critical districts in Mogadishu, and AMISOM 
continues to be considered the principal protagonist in battles with Al Shabaab. AMISOM is in the process of 
expanding its troop size from 8,000 to 12,000 to support stabilizing Mogadishu. Civilian casualties are high, 
with ICRC reporting 6,000 war-wounded civilians in 2010 (40% women or children) up from 2,800 in 2008. 
A major offensive by Al Shabaab in June 2009 dramatically restricted the TFG presence in Mogadishu and 
other areas of Somalia. However, a different trend was established in late February 2011 when the TFG 
forces and AMISOM conducted a coordinated offensive against Al Shabaab which resulted in securing and 
holding significant territorial gains in Mogadishu. The offensive includes parallel fighting along the EthiopianSomali border between Al Sunnah Wal Jammah and other pro-TFG militia, supported by regional actors, 
against Al Shabaab. Civilian and military casualties have been heavy in this last period of conflict. Al Shabaab
3has responded to the current fighting with mass recruitment involving child combatants, in a context where 
gross school enrolments for Somalia were 31 percent in 2006 (Source PES 2006/2007). 
With TFG and AMISOM security forces increasing their control in Mogadishu, expectations for peace 
dividends in the immediate and long term will be high for residents who have lacked basic public services 
from either the state administration or the government. Much of the Mogadishu zone of influence of the 
TFG is patrolled by clan-based militias which AMISOM relies on to buffer their forces, and which have no 
formal role within the TFG security structure, often resulting in increased clashes among them. Concerns by 
the current TFG over the extension of their term and the transition period have dominated political 
discourse. Concerns persist that it may prove difficult to sustain or consolidate the gains made by TFG forces 
and AMISOM during a continued period of political crisis within the Transitional Institutions. 
Al Shabaab has become the most powerful Somali military force in the country and exercises varying degrees 
of control over the biggest territory, including almost all of southern Somalia and about half of Mogadishu. 
Al Shabaab’s ongoing insurgency against AMISOM is currently the main source of armed conflict. The group 
has lost much of the public support (both in the country and in the Diaspora) it once enjoyed, owing to an 
increasing perception of foreign influence and, and as a result of appalling human rights abuse in areas it 
controls, including recruitment and use of children, abductions, rape and sexual violence against children and 
attacks on schools, in violation of international law. Al Shabaab’s interests vary from Al Qaida’s global jihad 
and the creation of a global caliphate, to invoking a nationalistic agenda to remove foreign forces such as 
AMISOM and a government dominated by Ethiopian and US interests. Al Shabaab has evolved over the past 
few years, and has incorporated other insurgent groups and appears to have an increasingly centralised 
command structure. A detailed analysis of Al Shabaab’s composition and their interests is on-going. 
Conflict Typology & the Underlying Causes 
Analysis undertaken for the ISF suggests that there are multiple drivers of conflict in Somalia, though most 
can be grouped into three overarching categories of conflict. Resource based conflict remains the most 
common reason for fighting. Clan clashes over the past twenty years were mainly triggered by struggles over 
valued resources – pasture, grazing rights, wells, and control of water rights, markets, airstrips, seaports, and 
international humanitarian or development aid and contracts. Others have been fuelled by disputes over 
political control of towns and districts. In the course of the past twenty years the loss of livelihoods and the 
growth of militias has generated large numbers of unemployed young men, who are easy recruits for criminal 
gangs and militia. In addition, private and some clan-based militias in and around Mogadishu are often the 
greatest source of chronic insecurity across Somalia motivated by resource accumulation. 
Citizenship, identity, and land rights remain unaddressed and are a powerful driving force for political and 
communal clashes. The protracted civil wars have generated economic conditions in which individuals benefit 
from continued warfare and lawlessness, such as the illegal charcoal exports to lucrative militia roadblocks 
and piracy. Politically, war criminals fear the prospect of revived systems of justice that could lead to their 
arrest, including the jihadists. The development of a “war economy” has combined with the predatory 
behaviour by successive governments and destroyed political trust, while creating the perception of the 
national government as “winner takes all” approach. Somalia’s regional administrations – most notably 
Puntland, secessionist Somaliland, and more recently Galmudug – are viewed as zones of relative peace, 
where disputes are settled through politics, not armed conflict. Even though these areas are not immune to 
conflict, they have had better local systems of conflict resolution than other parts of the country. 
4The Somali crisis is deeply entangled in a wider regional conflict that includes the unresolved EthiopiaEritrea war and the Ethiopian military against the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF). An underlying 
cause for concern are Ethiopia’s legitimate security concerns along its border with Somalia, made more acute 
by a past history of Somali irredentism directed at ethnically Somali-inhabited eastern Ethiopia. The general 
Somali political rhetoric remains focused on an anti-Ethiopia agenda. 
Linked to the global counter-terrorism efforts, Somalia is one of the major beneficiaries of the US-led 
counter-terrorism efforts. Over the past two decades Somalia witnessed the rise of an Islamic Awareness 
Movement which led to the ideological jihadist Islamism – an extremist movement embroiled in the wider 
‘global war on terror’. At the national level this was given a dramatic boost by the Ethiopian occupation of 
2007-08 and hundreds or thousands of youth joined Al Shabaab as a result. The intolerant strains of this 
religious ideology tend to enflame conflict as they leave little room for compromise and co-existence with 
other ideologies. However, the extremists attract a cadre of fighters who purport to transcend clan lines and 
who are much more committed, disciplined, and willing to die than fighters in Somali clan militias and 
government forces. Counter-terrorism partnerships with armed non-state actors who are commissioned to 
fight the extremist come at a cost, as these actors develop a vested interest in undermining state-building, 
since their value to the external actor hinges on the continued ineffectiveness of government security forces. 
C. The UN’s Combined Mandate 
UN agencies, funds and programmes have been operational in Somalia for over 50 years. They carry out 
activities that help alleviate poverty and suffering, encourage development and mitigate the effects of the 
conflict on the Somali people. The UNCT comprises 22 agencies, funds and programmes each with their own 
mandates: FAO, ILO, IOM, OHCHR, UNAIDS, UNDP, UNDSS, UNESCO, UNFPA, UNHABITAT, 
UNHCR, UNICEF, UNIFEM, UNMAS, UNOCHA, UNODC, UNOPS, UNPOS, UNV, WFP, WHO, 
World Bank. The main focus of the UNCT is outlined in the five year UN Somalia Assistance Strategy 
(UNSAS) which focuses on social services provision, including the humanitarian needs; livelihoods and 
poverty reduction; good governance and human security. 
UNPOS was established in April 1995. It is currently mandated by UN Security Council Resolutions 
(UNSCRs) 1910, 1872, 1863, 1814 and 1964 to facilitate national reconciliation and support the establishment 
of lasting peace and stability in Somalia. UNPOS is also mandated to support good governance and rule of 
law and the re-establishment of inclusive Somali security forces, and to support the TFG in combating illicit 
arms trafficking, disarmament, demobilization and reintegration (DDR), justice and corrections capacities. 
UNPOS jointly with UNODC has a mandate to coordinate counter-piracy initiatives. OHCHR is integrated 
into UNPOS with a mandate to monitor and report on human rights. At a broader level, UNSCR 1964 
endorsed the UN strategy, detailed in the 16 April 2009 report of the Secretary-General to the Security 
Council (S/2009/210), to set out an incremental approach whereby the United Nations would pursue its key 
strategic objectives in the political, security and humanitarian/recovery tracks while continuing to work 
towards the deployment of a peacekeeping operation at the appropriate time.
In addition, the UN Security Council has also mandated the UN Support Office for AMISOM (UNSOA) 
under UNSCR 1910 and 1964 to provide a logistical support package to AMISOM including equipment and 
services, but not transfer of funds. This includes providing vital provisions like food, water, fuel, evacuation 
services and medical supplies, public information as well as construction works aimed at improving the living 
5and working environment for AMISOM. A UN Trust Fund to help AMISOM’s mandate implementation 
was established until a UN Peacekeeping Operation is deployed. 
The table below reflects the key conflict variables (recognizing equifinality/causal reciprocity1) as highlighted 
in the ISF commissioned conflict analysis in January 2011, and looks at possible peacebuilding options for 
UN engagement. The conflict variables are grouped under five thematic areas which form the basis of this 
ISF; a limited political process, fragmented security sector, poor governance and rule of law, poor social 
services, and fragile economic development and livelihoods. The options for UN engagement highlighted in 
italics are the priority results and tasks articulated in the ISF Strategic Objectives.

6D. UN Vision for Somalia, Common Principles and Strategic Objectives 
UN Vision for Somalia 
The United Nations Joint Vision for Somalia is a stable and secure environment, respectful of the human 
rights, rule of law, and conducive to sustainable peace, reconciliation and socio-economic development for 
the benefit of all Somalis. 
Strategic Objectives and Priority Results 
To contribute to this longer-term vision, the UN team in Somalia seeks to achieve the following mediumterm Strategic Objectives, and short term (12 months) results: 
Strategic Objective 1: Broad-based agreement on a new political dispensation with greater 
legitimacy is attained 
Result 1.1 A constitutional framework based on public participation and consultation is adopted 
Result 1.2 A political outreach and negotiations strategy on the peace process is agreed, with wider Somali participation and ownership 
Result 1.3 A strategy for parliamentary reform is agreed 
Armed robbery and piracy off the coast of Somalia Illegal fishing and toxic dumping; 
War economy and statelessness benefiting limited actors National frameworks on illicit practices; mapping of business community 
Livestock and agricultural sectors; private investments and public-private 
partnerships; frameworks for natural resource management
Extreme resource scarcity and poverty
Destruction of economic infrastructure Infrastructure reconstruction; livelihoods; national frameworks

Capacity building; anti-corruption frameworks; legal frameworks on 
accountability; harmonizing sector policies

7Strategic Objective 2: Governance structures and processes function more effectively to incentivise 
peace with social justice 
Result 2.1 Core governance frameworks and processes are more responsive and accountable to the Somali people 
Result 2.2 Policy and legal frameworks that improve access to formal and informal justice systems are agreed, in line with 
international human rights standards 
Result 2.3 Transparency, accountability and anti-corruption legal frameworks that ensure self executing oversight over 
TFI’s are developed 
Result 2.4 Political and legal frameworks for equitable access to environmental and natural resources are developed. 
Strategic Objective 3: Community safety and security are improved in areas of TFG control, 
Somaliland, Puntland and emerging administrations 
Result 3.1 District security structures and processes are strengthened 
Result 3.2 Community security and stabilisation activities in Mogadishu are enhanced and gender sensitive 
Result 3.3 Somalia National Security Sector development framework established through a consultative process that 
includes women 
Result 3.4 Civilians benefit from increased and sustained protection against the effects of military operations in South 
Central, and parties to the conflict are held accountable for compliance with international humanitarian law 
Strategic Objective 4:The delivery of basic social services is continued and expanded, applying 
gender and conflict-sensitive approaches 
Result 4.1 At least one existing programme per sector reviewed for conflict-sensitivity, gender equity and peace-promoting potential and adjusted accordingly. 
Result 4.2 UN communications strategy reviewed and updated to enhance transparency and accountability and to ensure accurate reflection of provision of services, with immediate emphasis on drought and displacement response. 
Result 4.3 Sector policies and plans, linked with clusters, are initiated in all social sectors and support coherence between national and regional authorities, with an immediate emphasis on drought and displacement. 
Strategic Objective 5: The TFG and relevant regional authorities develop national economic policies 
and strategies that provide equitable growth and address immediate conflict drivers 
Result 5.1: National working group on private investment is established with sub-groups to address public-private 
partnership and private investment code of conduct. 
Result 5.2: Decent work is created for a minimum of 2,000 youth and women in identified locations of heightened 
conflict where employment creation will lessen conflict. 
Result 5.3: National fora are established to work on strategies for addressing charcoal trade, Illegal Unreported 
Unregulated fishing, human smuggling and trafficking, and port activities.
8Common Principles 
The UN in Somalia will work in accordance with the following principles: 
'Do no harm': UN operations should emphasize conflict and context sensitivity to avoid inducing conflict 
through the introduction of humanitarian, recovery and development assistance. 
Humanitarian principles: Humanitarian aid will be provided according to need alone and in accordance with 
humanitarian principles of humanity, neutrality, impartiality, operational independence. 
Aid Effectiveness: UN and partners should uphold good practices and development aid principles (e.g. relevant 
parts of the Paris Declaration and Fragile States Principles as appropriate to the context). 
Accountability and Performance: Ensure that the UN, partners and all Somali institutions that receive donor 
funding adhere to agreed standards of performance, accountability and transparency. 
Ownership: All UN strategies should ensure Somali people at the centre of all programmes. 
Gender Equality and Women Empowerment: UN operations should ensure the inclusion and participation of 
women, and that programming is gender-sensitive. 
Increased UN personnel deployment to Somalia: UNPOS, UNSOA and UNCT should incrementally increase 
deployment of personnel from Nairobi to Somalia, in order to improve engagement with the national and 
local authorities, strengthen contextual analysis, and improve programme monitoring. 
Strategic Objectives and Results 
1. Broad-based agreement on a new political dispensation with greater legitimacy is attained – Lead: 
UNPOS
The past few years of Somalia’s transition have been marked by the absence of: meaningful consultations and 
outreach by the TFG to various Somali actors; engagement with the regional administrations and other 
stakeholders; and the political will to provide services to populations in Mogadishu and beyond. The recent 
unilateral extension by the Parliament for three years beyond the end of the transition in August 2011, and 
the current dispute between the Transitional Federal Parliament (TFP) and the TFG about the extension have 
given the impression to many Somalis that their leaders are focused on their own survival, rather than on the 
needs of the people. Hence the current Transitional Federal Institutions (TFIs) enjoy very little support 
amongst the Somali people. In order to promote unity among the Somali people, and to ensure that the 
Somali Institutions are genuinely representative and legitimate, there is an urgent need for the TFIs to consult 
with all relevant stakeholders in their decision-making process for a post-transition political dispensation. 
Without such consideration, there is a danger that any new dispensation could lead to further fragmentation 
and disillusionment among the people of Somalia. Hence, the UN will prioritize the following results: 
1.1 A constitutional framework based on public participation and consultation is adopted 
The Constitution and outreach and reconciliation are the most important outstanding tasks for the TFIs. 
There is agreement amongst Somalis and international actors that the Constitution can serve to underwrite a 
Somali identity and spur nation-building. It should, among other things enshrine basic rights, solidify a system 
of checks and balances and operationalize the principle of decentralization. In order to ensure that the 
Constitution is the product of the Somali people, key stakeholders, including civil society with a particular 
9focus on women and vulnerable groups must be consulted. Timing is critical, and a sequencing of important 
milestones will drive the process towards, and possibly beyond the August 2011 timeline. The constitution 
process is inherently political and must be carefully sequenced to help promote political transformation and 
peace consolidation. 
1.2 A political outreach and negotiations strategy on the peace process is agreed, with wider Somali 
participation and ownership 
While the Djibouti process has made significant progress, such as devising a Constitution roadmap, Somali 
endorsement of the peace process remains limited. Consultations and participation by the TFIs and multiple 
segments of the Somali society has been missing. Continued exclusion risks losing the support of the Somali 
people in the future dispensations. As a result, there is a general condition for reform to ensure broader 
(political) consultations with the Somali people to enable them to shape their future. It will be important to 
support the TFIs to engage more broadly with Somalis to facilitate Somali ownership of the process. 
1.3 A strategy for parliamentary reform is agreed 
While a number of technical tasks lie ahead of the TFIs, broad political reforms are necessary to gain the trust 
of the Somali people. The TFIs have been limping along during the transitional period, with a poor track 
record in implementing the key transitional tasks and frameworks. The High Level Committee (HLC), 
established in the Djibouti Agreement to address political matters, is an ideal forum for the Somali leadership 
to take back ownership of the process, toward a post-transition political dispensation. The HLC will also 
facilitate increased coordination between the international community and Somalis. 
2. Governance structures and processes function more effectively to incentivise peace with social 
justice – Lead: UNSAS Outcome 3: UNDP + UNPOS
Good governance provides the foundation for the maintenance of a peaceful environment. It enables broad 
based economic growth, social justice as well as the administration of security and social services. The 
predatory nature of the Siad Barre regime and the aftermath of its collapse led to a general mistrust of the 
central government amongst many Somalis. Subsequent transitional governments, based on a series of peace 
agreements have similar track records and have often contributed to this lack of trust. Since 1991, local and 
traditional and hybrid governance structures have often proved more effective and deemed more legitimate as 
sources of authority by Somalis. State-building efforts must be recalibrated in recognition of this fact. Hence, 
the UN will prioritize the following results: 
2.1 Core governance frameworks and processes are more responsive and accountable to the Somali 
people 
One of the significant constraints to strengthening governance and service delivery in Somalia is the current 
lack of coherent policy and legal frameworks regarding horizontal and vertical institutional government 
structures and links to informal structures. Such policy and legal frameworks must flow from deep and 
enduring political agreements, and be supported by sound technical arrangements. The emergence of regional 
administrations aspiring to sub-national status within a federal structure is increasing, and will need to be 
managed within a process-based framework that ensures cooperation, flexibility and which minimizes the 
potential for further fragmentation and conflict. Indeed, the process of federalizing or decentralizing the 
country should ultimately enhance national unity and result in a common shared vision, supported by 
devolved power so as to allow locally specific and appropriate governance. To ensure that accountability is 
systematically imbedded at all levels of government, the framework will ensure adequate separation of powers 
to ensure checks and balances. Political actors in Somalia compete for government positions because of the 
access that this provides to land, money and power, and this must be addressed. 
102.2 Policy and legal frameworks that improve access to formal and informal justice systems are 
agreed, in line with international human rights standards 
An array of formal and informal justice actors exist throughout Somalia. To strengthen complementarities 
among legal systems and ensure that the justice sector as a whole makes progress towards upholding 
international human rights standards, the UN will develop policy and legal frameworks to strengthen and 
harmonize formal and informal justice systems and sources of law. This will be done through the 
Constitution and associated legal reforms. A strong, independent and functional judicial branch is essential to 
balanced and democratic governance. The UN will address justice sector governance by focusing initially on 
improving coherence and harmony of legal traditions, in an effort to strengthen the foundation for adherence 
to the rule of law and international human rights standards. 
2.3 Transparency, accountability and anti-corruption legal frameworks that ensure self executing 
oversight over TFIs are developed 
Principles of transparency, accountability and participation (“TAP”) are best enforced when institutional 
capacity is strengthened and strong anti-corruption ethics and legal frameworks are in place. This is 
particularly so in Somalia, a fragile and developing state where fiscal and other resources are scarce, and 
diversion of resources has a particularly devastating impact on populations. The UN will focus on 
establishing an agreed policy and legal framework, with an emphasis on embedded implementation timelines 
across government institutions. 
2.4 Political and legal frameworks for equitable access to environmental and natural resources are 
developed 
Environmental issues, natural resources management and distribution of land and property rights are deep 
rooted and complex conflict drivers in Somalia. These issues have received scant attention and almost no 
intervention to date in Somalia. An agreed environmental management and protection framework is an 
essential component of problem solving around natural resource management. This priority result is linked 
to livelihoods and economic development, and will require particularly coherent UN action. 
3. Community safety and security are improved in areas of TFG control, Somaliland, Puntland and 
emerging administrations – Lead: UNPOS and UNDP 
This objective aims to improve the safety and security of civilians affected by the conflict, and particularly of 
women, children and other vulnerable sectors, in priority regions, particularly in Mogadishu, in support of the 
UN’s political objectives. Key challenges in the security sector include access, TFG transition, the emergence 
of regional administrations and the absence of a revised NSSP. The lack or limited access to Somalia, in 
particular in South Central, hampers the UN's ability to effectively monitor and oversee interventions in the 
security sector. Reported violations by armed groups military forces are rampant but are difficult to monitor 
and effectively address. Children are especially affected by forced recruitment, rape and sexual violence, 
abductions, displacement, and attacks on their schools. The lack of clarity on the post transition structure 
raises concerns for the security sector in terms of change in interlocutors and priorities of security sector 
institutions. While the emergence of regional administrations will be addressed under the Strategic Objective 
on Governance and the Rule of Law, it remains a critical concern for community level safety and security. 
Building community trust and confidence towards the TFG will continue to be a challenge as the loosely 
aligned forces to the TFG lack clear command and control structures. The security sector remains a highly 
11scrutinized and crowded programmatic environment which is further challenged by divergent views and 
priorities within the international community. Hence, the UN will prioritize the following results: 
3.1 District security structures and processes are strengthened 
This key result area will support the strengthening of district security structures recognizing that needs and 
character of the these structures will vary in the different regions and between urban and rural communities. 
Joint mapping and analysis of community district committee structures will ensure interventions are 
effectively targeted and implemented. Based in part on the results of the mapping, emphasis will be placed on 
strengthening relationships and collaboration between AMISOM stability operations, district level actors and 
policy coordination at the level of the Joint Security Committee. 
3.2 Community security and stabiliation activities in Mogadishu are enhanced and gender sensitive 
Given the rapidly changing environment in Mogadishu, security stabilisation activities are intended to help 
build trust and confidence in priority communities over the next 12 months. The priority initiatives set out 
below will build on the joint mapping/analysis of community and district committee structures to ensure 
targeted and effective interventions. The four priority interventions include an inter agency initiative targeting 
‘youth at risk’ which will focus on prevention of youth recruitment, while profiling of defectors and the 
development of an emergency response plan that supports demobilization of ex militia. Mine action efforts 
in support of police EOD and AMISOM explosive stockpile management, together with the provision of 
logistical support to AMISOM (including additional 4,000 troops) and humanitarian amine action support 
seeks to reinforce the capacity of key actors responsible for safety and security. 
3.3 Somalia National Security Sector development framework established through a consultative 
process that includes women 
In support of improved security and safety, efforts will focus on the review, adoption and implementation of 
a National Security and Stabilisation Plan (NSSP). Security sector assessments will be completed in 
Somaliland and Puntland, complementing assessment completed in Mogadishu in 2010. In addition, priority 
support to the police will be emphasized, including the completion of a police registration system, 
continuation of training at all levels, provision of support to stipends and the development of a maritime 
police force. This result also includes a key analytical component which will support joint mapping and 
analysis of armed groups and quantification of existing surveys. Regulation of private security companies by 
regional authorities will be supported through provision of technical advice on requisite legal frameworks. 
3.4 Civilians benefit from increased and sustained protection against the effects of military 
operations in South Central, and parties to the conflict are held accountable for compliance with 
international humanitarian law 
The UN will seek to encourage parties to the conflict, in line with IHL and human rights standards, to take all 
feasible precautions to spare civilians from the effects of the hostilities, and to mitigate the consequences of 
displacement. The UN will engage with parties to the conflict to underscore the importance of compliance 
with applicable international humanitarian law, as a means of reducing the risks civilians face during armed 
conflict. This will include engagement in dialogue and action plans with all parties to conflict for the release 
of children and ending grave violations against children; and review of tactical directives to minimize civilian 
casualties. The UN will also support the provision of legal assistance to civilians. 
124. The delivery of basic social services is continued and expanded, applying gender and conflictsensitive approaches – Lead: UNSAS Outcome 1: UNICEF
Supporting the equitable provision of social services2 to the people of Somalia reinforces peace-building 
efforts and contributes to societal stability. The role of the Somali government in the provision of social 
services is unclear, despite the political interest that could emanate from that. However, the UN advises that it 
should remain one of oversight and regulation rather than direct service delivery. Approaches to social 
services provision must build on public-private partnerships given the role the private sector and the 
community already play, in the absence of a government one. 
The UN strategy is to broaden support for equitable rights and access to social services for all Somalis. As a 
result of two decades of deprivation and limited access to social services, women, youth and children3 deserve 
a special focus by the UN. Given the lack of a central approach, the UN is also committed to supporting an 
overarching policy for social service provision that improves coherence between the central level and regional 
authorities. Hence, the UN will prioritize the following results: 
4.1 At least one existing programme per sector reviewed for conflict-sensitivity, gender equity and 
peace-promoting potential and adjusted accordingly. 
Through the ISF, agencies agreed to review one existing programme per sector for conflict sensitivity across 
all social service sectors. As this commitment could entail a significant adjustment of current implementation 
methods, and some additional resources may be required, a coherent advocacy approach towards the donors 
is also required. 
4.2 UN communications strategy is reviewed and updated to enhance transparency and 
accountability and to ensure accurate reflection of provision of services, with immediate 
emphasis on drought and displacement response 
This result will focus on developing systematic advocacy messages on the UN response in Somalia targeting 
Somalis, government, donors and the broader UN. For the larger UN system, the UN Information Group is 
developing a strategy to raise awareness on UN operations. Existing UNSOA/UNPOS/ UNCT information 
mechanisms should also be used to the extent possible. The messages will also support increased 
accountability for results and transparency of UN operations. 
4.3 Sector policies and plans, linked with clusters, are initiated in all social sectors and support 
coherence between national and regional authorities, with an immediate emphasis on drought 
and displacement 
The UN system is committed to ensure a more coherent approach through support to sector planning, and to 
improving equity in access. A special focus is placed on vulnerable groups, women and girls and the displaced 
population is a priority. 
                                                           
2 The social service sector encompasses the health/nutrition, education, WASH, food, shelter, welfare and basic access infrastructure sectors. 
3 Estimates indicate that children make up 50 percent of the total population and the youth population between the age of 15 to 29 comprise about 27 percent ( 2.3 million) of 
the total population in Somalia while those below the age of 29 account for 73 percent of the total population based on the Socio- economic Survey 2002 and UNDP 2005-
2010 projection estimates.
135. The TFG and relevant regional authorities develop national economic policies and strategies that 
provide equitable growth and address immediate conflict drivers – Lead: UNSAS Outcome 2: FAO
The conflict in Somalia has an economic dimension, and the war economy has been one of the continuous 
features of the conflict. The conflict in Somalia has been associated with an absence of functioning 
institutions of state for two decades. Somalia’s return to stability cannot rely on politics and security alone. It 
also depends on addressing the economy as a driver of the conflict and, at the same time, as a catalyst for 
peace. Thus the role of the political economy and economic development is key to the restoration of peace 
and stability in Somalia. In this nexus it is important to consider the multiple dimensions of widespread 
inequality in Somalia and to aim at managing and transforming the conflict through a process of 
empowerment (social, economic and political) of youth and vulnerable groups. 
Somalia has presented a challenge to the political economy and has undermined the nexus between political 
institutions and environment, and the economic system both domestically and regionally. It has affected 
international trade through piracy and investment in the region, making it expensive for domestic and 
multinational corporations to conduct business. In an international system of nation-states, trade must be 
regulated, and Somalia has limited success in this regard. If trade remains unregulated, this can be a cause of 
conflict and recession domestically and regionally. Political economy and economic development are the 
nexus for strengthening peace processes and establishing a functioning state. 
In this context, the Strategic Objective focuses on developing national economic policies and strategies that 
provide equitable growth and address immediate conflict drivers. Priority Results focus is on all of Somalia 
however based on the conflict drivers an increased focus on South Central Somalia will be a priority. Based 
on the twelve month timeframe, the focus in the results is about setting up processes, and to create a 
conducive environment for these process to take place. Hence, the UN will prioritize the following results: 
5.1 National working group on private investment is established with sub-groups to address publicprivate partnership and private investment code of conduct 
The first priority result looks at creating an enabling environment for increased private and foreign direct 
investments in Somalia and public and private sector partnership, while recognizing that the political actors 
are also economic actors. Regulation should be used to deal with monopolistic markets, ensure that the public 
sector has a role vis-à-vis all facets of the private sector, and to avoid a situation where political actors have an 
incentive to gain political authority in order to control economic resources. A code of conduct between the 
public sector, private sector and donor community could be developed working off the progress made during 
the “Istanbul Conference” in 2010. 
5.2 Decent work is created for a minimum of 2,000 youth and women in identified locations of 
heightened conflict where employment creation will lessen conflict 
The second priority result focuses on the opportunity to create decent work for Somalis employment which is 
vital to short-term stability, reintegration, economic growth and sustainable peace and should balance the 
need for a quick action with the importance of sustainable impact. Employment creation should deliver the 
economic benefits and peace dividends to the affected population with particular attention to reducing 
inequalities towards women and youth. The United Nations can act as a facilitator and as a catalyst for the 
process of transforming opportunities into reality. 
145.3 National fora are established to work on strategies for addressing charcoal trade, Illegal 
Unreported Unregulated fishing, human smuggling and trafficking, and port activities 
The third priority result focuses on establishing national fora on strategies for addressing Illegal Unreported 
Unregulated fishing (IUU), human smuggling and trafficking, charcoal trade, and port services. The political 
economy of charcoal and IUU requires increased UN involvement, particularly in collating and analyzing the 
myriad of studies in these areas. Human smuggling and trafficking should be addressed in the context of 
economic development. Overall, there is a need to ensure that Somalia is part of key conventions and 
protocols, and that the UN system supports Somalia attain these. 
E. Remaining Challenges 
UN Options for Transition and Post-Transition: The consensus by IGAD to support an extension of 
parliament somewhat undermined broader consultations on the issue of parliamentary reform. The prevailing 
view among the international community in Wilton Park in February 2011 was in favour of a one year 
extension. The TFG has proposed a one-two year extension for itself, making the argument that they need to 
deliver against their recently developed “Road map”. it remains unclear how the Transition will end, and what 
form the post-transitional dispensation will take. 
The Constitution-Making Process: A priority issue for the UN is the support to the Constitution-making 
process. While the UN had planned to support Somalis lead the completion of the Constitution by August 
2011, broader technical and political consultations are required at a scale that is likely to extend the adoption 
of the Constitution to August 2012. Although the Transitional Charter provided for adoption by referendum 
other forms of adoption are also being considered. 
Mogadishu Stabilisation: The ongoing offensive in Mogadishu led by TFG forces aided by AMISOM and 
regional actors could secure Mogadishu in the near future. A joint UN stabilisation plan to support Somalis 
address the overall needs in Mogadishu is urgently required, acknowledging that humanitarian assistance 
would only be provided based on need. The Mogadishu rehabilitation plan could be the basis for this plan, 
incorporating other sector support It is unclear if the offensive will secure and sustain stability in Mogadishu, 
and if it will extend deeper in the south to other areas where Al Shabaab are present. There is a need to clarify 
what “stabilisation” includes with regards to the provision of services and security. 
Engagement with the TFG and Regional Administrations: The implications of the ‘dual track approach’ 
launched by the United States in September 2010 remain unclear to the UN. While the UN is mandated to 
respect the unity and territorial integrity of Somalia, there is an urgent need for UNPOS to prepare a proposal 
for the UN and the international community on engagement with regional administration, as well as how to 
get the support of the TFG in this regard. Nevertheless, establishing presences in Puntland and Somaliland is 
agreed as a window of opportunity to look at emerging needs, and supports coherence and coordination of 
policies across the regions.  
Role of TFG as a service provider or facilitator: The UN sees the role of the TFG as both a provider of 
services and a facilitator/regulator, depending on the sectors. The TFG have prioritised maintenance of law 
and order such as judiciary, justice, rule of law and police services. Other basic services such as water, refuse 
collection, education and health, etc. are currently provided by other actors. A discussion within the UN and 
with the TFG is required to clarify the role of government as a facilitator and service provider. 
Engagement with all parties to the conflict: In Somalia, Armed opposition Groups (AoG) control over 50 
percent of the country. One AoG in particular was designated under UNSCR 1844 as a terrorist organisation. 
15UNSCR 1916, grants a ‘humanitarian carve out’ and allows all humanitarian agencies to continue operating to 
assist those in need in areas controlled by designated terrorist groups. Non humanitarian agencies cannot 
engage with AoGs that are formally designated as terrorist organisations. However, it is important to note 
that the listing of the Al-Shabaab and the newly merged Hizbul Islam on the annexes of the SecretaryGeneral’s reports on children and armed conflict calls for the engagement by the UN with these parties for 
the purposes of preparation and implementation of action plans to address child recruitment and other grave 
violations for which these parties are cited, as required by Security Council resolutions 1539 (2004), 1612 
(2005) and 1882 (2009). The Security Council also requests that the national government facilitate such 
dialogue. There is a recognised need to understand AoGs and their interests, and to identify ways to engage 
with them at the appropriate levels. 
Role of UNSOA/AMISOM: UNSOA has a Security Council mandate to deliver a logistical support package 
to AMISOM. This support is critical in enabling AMISOM fulfil its mandate to support the transitional 
federal institutions, implement a national security plan, train the Somali security forces, facilitate the provision 
of humanitarian assistance and to create conducive conditions for long-term stabilisation, reconstruction and 
development of Somalia. Most of UNSOA's support activities are funded through assessed contributions of 
Member States of the United Nations. Additional funding is provided through a trust fund created to finance 
those aspects of support to AMISOM that can not be funded through assessed contributions. In addition to 
facilitating the provision of humanitarian assistance, including repatriation and reintegration of refugees and 
resettlement of IDPs, AMISOM's mandated role in supporting disarmament and stabilisation efforts are seen 
as critical civil-support activities for the peacekeeping mission. There is a need for internal UN discussion on 
the role of the UNSOA support to AMISOM’s ‘humanitarian’ mandate. 
F. Coordination, Implementation and Monitoring Arrangements 
Each of the five priority Strategic Objectives in the ISF will have a working group to coordinate planning and 
implementation of tasks, share information, and monitor progress. The five thematic working groups will 
oversee the achievement of the results as they contribute to the Strategic Objectives and the broader vision. 
 
The coordination of three out of the five ISF Strategic Objectives utilizes the UNSAS outcome groups of 
"Social Services”; “Poverty Reduction and Livelihoods” and “Good Governance and Human Security”. 
These groups are complimented by two newly established working groups to coordinate ‘Political’ and 
‘Security Sector’. 
SPG, UNCT and JPU Coordination 
• The expanded Senior Policy Group (SPG) under the chairmanship of the SRSG, will monitor overall 
implementation of the ISF on a quarterly basis, and provide management guidance and interventions as 
necessary based on advice from the working groups. The SPG membership includes representatives from 
UNPOS, UNSOA, and the UNCT. The JPU will continue to provide secretariat support to the SPG. 
• The UNCT under the chairmanship of the RC/HC will receive the minutes of the SPG and defer 
relevant policy issues to the SPG following discussion at the UNCT. 
• The SPG primarily, and the UNCT as required will task the JPU to undertake preparatory work for policy 
discussions in close coordination with the relevant stakeholders. To facilitate these discussions, the JPU 
will prepare a forward agenda for SPG discussions in consultation with the SPG and UNCT members. 
16• The JPU will coordinate quarterly meetings with the Outcome Leads through the existing UNSAS Task 
Force which will be expanded to include the JPU and the chairs of Political and Security Sectors. In the 
event additional meetings are needed, the JPU will call on all working group chairs to convene. 
The Working Groups 
• Each of the working groups will ensure, within their line of operation, that the results and key activities 
are linked to other planned results of the wider ISF, the UNSAS, UNPOS and UNSOA Results Based 
Budgets (RBB). To this end, the JPU should have standing representation in each of the working groups. 
• All working groups will develop risk management options and proactively advise the SPG of any 
obstacles and/or delays to results delivery, including recommended remedial measures to mitigate 
obstacles/delays and the operational and/or other consequences. 
• Each of the working groups will contribute inputs to quarterly consolidated reports on results delivery, 
including obstacles/delays. These consolidated reports will be compiled by the JPU for review at regular 
meetings of the SPG. Templates for monitoring will be provided by the JPU to all working groups (see 
Monitoring below). 
Improved collection, analysis and sharing of information 
• To improve information flow on humanitarian, development, political and military issues between 
UNPOS, UNSOA and UNCT, both UNPOS and UNSOA should regularly attend (at senior levels) the 
UNCT, SMT, and SMT working group. Likewise, representatives of the UNCT should attend the SPG. 
• The establishment of a Joint Mission Analysis Centre (JMAC) in UNPOS that will coordinate with 
UNSOA and UNCT agencies is recommended. The JMAC will identify flashpoints and produce 
integrated analyses and recommendations for the SRSG and senior management in real time on political 
developments, security risks and threats. The JMAC modalities of work with the Security Information 
and Operations Centre (SIOC) will be explored. 
• To further strengthen information sharing and coordination on issues covered by both the mission and 
the UNCT, and when agreeable to both, programmes will be co-located. 
Contingency Planning 
• Inter-agency contingency planning will continue to be updated, including input from UNPOS and 
UNSOA to provide effective responses to local conflicts and displacement, considerable political turmoil 
and increased military action. 
Monitoring 
• The monitoring of the ISF Strategic Objectives and working groups will be supported by the JPU and the

Annex 1: Preparations for the ISF 
The ISF is informed by a combination of analysis of the situation in Somalia. In addition the following 
documents were referenced: the 2005/2006 JNA; 2008 UN Strategic Assessment; the 2011-2015 
UNSAS; 2011 CAP; ongoing FSNAU reports; CAP and a external reports including from International 
Crisis Group, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Interpeace. The ISF also draws on recent 
UN scenario planning conducted for the CAP, the UNSAS and for the UNPOS strategy. 
In preparation for the ISF, the JPU conducted an analysis of existing UN frameworks and strategies. The 
analysis of existing frameworks juxtaposed by the conflict analysis indicated five key thematic priority 
areas for UN engagement in Somalia. These are: Political process and national reconciliation; 
security sector; social services; governance and rule of law; economic development and 
livelihoods. While existing frameworks outline in detail what the UN agencies and missions in Somalia 
will undertake in terms of activities, the ISF allows the UN to re-prioritize existing key objectives and 
results to address peace consolidation in Somalia in the next 12 months. 
The main UN planning frameworks analyzed were: UNPOS Security Council mandates, UNPOS Results 
Based Budgeting (RBB), UNPOS Draft Strategy; the UNSOA Security Council mandates and RBB; the 
UN Somali Assistance Strategy (UNSAS) and; the Consolidated Appeal Process (CAP) for UN 
humanitarian agencies and NGOs and the AU/IGAD/UNPOS Strategy. The UNSAS is based on the 
nationally owned reconstruction and development plan (RDP) as is the Interim Strategic Note (ISN) of 
the World Bank and the Joint Strategy Paper (JSP) of the EU and Norway. The TFG roadmap, draft 
Somaliland and Puntland development plans were referenced in the analysis. 
During the development of the ISF the UN consulted internally on a regular basis with a number of 
stakeholders including the IMPP Working Group, the Integrated Task Force, UNCT agencies, and the 
SPG. Externally, the ISF objectives and results were discussed with key donors to Somalia, NGO 
partners and AMISOM. The TFG and regional authorities consultation is considered through the 
consultations on the political processes and the UNSAS. 
25Annex 2: SWOT Analysis 
Strengths
• Experienced UN Team with a diverse set of 
skills in political, programming and military 
work 
• Long history of UN programming in all areas 
of Somalia, Puntland, Somaliland etc. 
• Strong UN international and national 
presence in Somaliland and Puntland and 
continued national staff presence in South 
Central with growing international staff 
numbers in Mogadishu 
Weaknesses
• Broad range of opinions across the UN about the 
relationship between state building and peacebuilding. 
• No international and nationally shared strategy 
regarding Somalia 
• Access limited due to security and liability issues 
• Incorrectly perceived as UN in exile 
• UN sometimes focused on processes 
(strategy/planning), rather than outcomes 
• UN sometimes over-influenced by competition for 
access to donor resources 
• Difficulties translating management commitment to 
staff action 
Opportunities
• End of transition period is an opportunity to 
review statebuilding in the Somalia context 
• Robust Somali private sector including 
Diaspora 
• ISF can refocus the UN on outcomes and 
establish clear division of responsibility 
within the UN about who works on 
overlapping issues 
• Increased international attention on Somalia 
means the pressure to deliver is high 
• Opportunity to streamline coordination 
mechanisms if the ISF is eventually 
incorporated in the UNSAS and one 
document is agreed 
Threats
• Dual Track approach and donor funding decisions 
related to the global financial crisis affecting access to 
recovery funding especially in Mogadishu 
• Negative perceptions of the UN and its 
operations/responses in country 
• Weak disunited TFG, perceived as focused on 
enriching itself that is facing an international crisis of 
confidence 
• Focus by donors and government on short-term quick 
impact projects at expense of long-term projects that 
could alter the status quo 
• Enduring stalemate in the capital in favour of 
insurgency groups 
• Insecurity impedes humanitarian access
